stories.title: Haze Alarm Bells Ring: Singapore Gets Ready Just In Case
stories.headline_kid: A regional weather watchtower has raised its haze alert, so Singapore is dusting off its haze action plan.
summary: Every year, forest fires in parts of Indonesia can send smoke drifting over to Singapore, making our sky look grey and hazy. A group called the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre watches the whole region for smoke and fires, a bit like a lifeguard watching the beach for danger. This week, they raised their alert to Level 2, which is the second-highest level, meaning the chance of haze reaching us has gone up.

This does not mean haze has arrived in Singapore yet. It means our government wants to be prepared, just like how you might pack an umbrella when the sky looks cloudy, even before it rains. Singapore has a haze task force that checks air quality, gets N95 masks ready, and reminds schools what to do if the air becomes unhealthy to breathe.

If haze does arrive, you might notice a smoky smell, hazy skies, and outdoor activities like PE or recess games being moved indoors. The government uses something called the PSI (Pollutant Standards Index) to measure how clean or dirty the air is, similar to how a thermometer measures temperature.

For now, everyone is just on standby. Singapore has dealt with haze before, so schools and families already know the drill: stay indoors more, drink water, and listen to updates from teachers or parents.

lenses.me: If the haze gets bad, your outdoor PE lessons or recess time outside might be moved indoors to protect your lungs.
lenses.family: Your family might need to buy or check N95 masks at home, just in case the air turns unhealthy.
lenses.friends: Your class might have indoor games instead of outdoor sports if the haze alert rises further.
lenses.nation: Singapore's haze task force works with hospitals, schools and transport services to keep everyone safe when smoky air blows in.
lenses.world: This shows how fires in one country can affect the air that millions of people breathe in nearby countries, reminding the region to work together.

stories.title: Old Bicycle Shops Struggle as App-Based Bike Sharing Takes Over
stories.headline_kid: Renting a bike from a beach shop used to be the only way — now an app can unlock one for you in seconds, and shop owners are worried.
summary: For many years, families cycling at places like East Coast Park would rent bicycles from small rental shops. Now, more people are using bike-sharing apps like HelloRide, where you simply scan a bicycle with your phone, ride it, and leave it anywhere in the zone when you're done.

This is convenient and often cheaper than renting from a shop for a whole day. Because of this, three rental shop owners told reporters they have had to make tough choices — some are downsizing (making their business smaller), some are diversifying (selling other things too, like drinks or bicycle accessories), and some are even thinking about closing down completely.
This is a bit like what happened when ride-hailing apps such as Grab became popular — some traditional taxi services found it harder to compete because the app was more convenient for customers.
The bicycle shop owners are not giving up though. Many are finding new ways to attract customers, such as offering special bikes for kids or family bundles that apps don't provide.

lenses.me: The next time you cycle at a park, you might notice more shared bikes from apps than rental shop bicycles.
lenses.family: Your family might find it cheaper and easier to use a bike-sharing app instead of renting from a shop during a weekend outing.
lenses.friends: Your friends might already be using bike-sharing apps for school trips or weekend rides with their families.
lenses.nation: This shows how new technology can change even small, traditional businesses in Singapore, pushing owners to adapt or struggle.
lenses.world: Similar changes are happening worldwide, where apps make renting things like bikes, scooters, or even umbrellas faster and cheaper than traditional shops.

stories.title: Lightning Strikes Football Field, Reminding Everyone About Outdoor Safety
stories.headline_kid: A football match in Thailand turned tragic when lightning struck the field, killing one player and injuring others — including a Malaysian.
summary: During a football match in Narathiwat, southern Thailand, lightning struck the pitch while players were still playing. Sadly, a Thai footballer died, and 12 other people were injured, including a player from Malaysia. The match was part of a regional tournament called the Golok FA Cup.

Lightning can strike very suddenly, even if it seems like the storm is still far away. This is why sports events, including school PE lessons in Singapore, are stopped immediately when thunder is heard or lightning is detected nearby.

In Singapore, schools use lightning detection systems that automatically warn teachers when lightning is within a certain distance, so outdoor activities can be paused before it becomes dangerous. This tragic accident is a reminder of why these safety rules exist, even though they can sometimes feel inconvenient when you just want to keep playing.
The incident has shocked football fans across Southeast Asia, and organisers of sports events are being reminded to always check weather warnings carefully before matches, especially outdoors.

lenses.me: The next time your PE teacher stops an outdoor game because of thunder, you'll understand exactly why it's such an important rule.
lenses.family: Your family might be extra careful about staying indoors during thunderstorms after hearing about this accident.
lenses.friends: Your classmates might talk about this news and appreciate why school outdoor activities pause during thunder warnings.
lenses.nation: Singapore's strict lightning safety rules in schools and sports events exist exactly to prevent tragedies like this one.
lenses.world: This sad accident reminds people across the world that lightning is a serious natural danger, especially during outdoor sports.

stories.title: Malaysia Promises to Protect Refugees If Sending Them Home Is Too Dangerous
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia says it won't send Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar if it means putting their lives in danger.
summary: The Rohingya are a group of people who had to flee their homes in Myanmar because of conflict and unfair treatment. Many of them have been living in nearby countries like Malaysia and Bangladesh for years, hoping to find safety.

Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim recently announced a plan to send 5,000 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, saying conditions there had improved. But this plan worried many people, because Myanmar can still be unsafe for the Rohingya.

This week, Malaysia's government said it would not force anyone to return if their lives would be at risk. This means officials will first check carefully whether it is truly safe before sending anyone back — similar to how a lifeguard would check the sea conditions before letting swimmers back in after a storm warning.

Singapore is part of the same region as Malaysia and Myanmar, through a group called ASEAN, where Southeast Asian countries work together. Issues like refugee safety affect how neighbouring countries cooperate and care for people in the region.

lenses.me: This story helps you understand that some children around the world don't have a safe home to return to, unlike you.
lenses.family: Your family might discuss how lucky you are to live in a safe and stable country like Singapore.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might talk about this in class discussions about kindness and helping people in need.
lenses.nation: Singapore, as part of ASEAN, cares about how neighbouring countries handle humanitarian issues like refugee safety, since regional stability matters to us too.
lenses.world: This shows how countries must balance their own rules with caring for people who have nowhere safe to go.

stories.title: From Old Letters to WeChat: Teochew Families Find Long-Lost Relatives
stories.headline_kid: Some Singaporeans are using DNA tests and a chat app to track down relatives their families lost touch with generations ago in China.
summary: Many Singaporeans have ancestors who came from Teochew, a region in China, many years ago. Over time, some families lost contact with relatives who stayed behind, sometimes because of old, faded letters that stopped being sent, or because of war and hard times long ago.

Recently, a popular Chinese movie called Dear You inspired more Singaporeans and Malaysians of Teochew descent to search for their roots. They are now turning to a volunteer network in China, using tools like DNA testing and the chat app WeChat, to trace long-lost family members.

Finding a distant cousin or great-aunt after so many years is like finishing a puzzle that has been missing pieces for decades. Volunteers on the ground in China help match clues from old letters, family names, and village records to reconnect families who thought they'd never meet again.
This story shows how technology and determination can bring families back together, even across countries and generations, reminding us how precious family history and roots can be.

lenses.me: You might ask your own grandparents or parents about where your family originally came from and if you have relatives you've never met.
lenses.family: Your family might feel inspired to research your own family tree or ancestry using similar tools.
lenses.friends: Your friends with Teochew or Chinese ancestry might share similar family history stories at home.
lenses.nation: Many Singaporeans have roots tracing back to China, and stories like this remind us how migration shaped our multicultural society.
lenses.world: This shows how modern technology like DNA testing and apps can help people reconnect across countries, even after many decades apart.
